definitions.meaning: read as arm-y support: a cloth loop that holds up an injured arm
a strap device for hurling stones, as David used against Goliath

explanation.surface: A question about what an army leans on to fire its rockets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army' is split as arm-y: something that supports an arm.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a bandage cradling a broken limb and a simple stone-throwing weapon.

clue.text: Drug needed for one of Macbeth's victims

definitions.text: Drug needed for one of Macbeth's victims

parts.words: Drug needed for one of Macbeth's victims
parts.note: Macbeth cries that he 'does murder sleep', so sleep is one of his victims, and a drug that brings it on is what it needs

explanation.surface: Someone prescribing medicine for a person attacked by Shakespeare's murderous king.
explanation.walkthrough: The victim is not Duncan or Banquo but sleep itself, which Macbeth says he has murdered.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleep-inducing medicine is the kind of drug that would revive slumber.

parts.note: sounds like a retired soldier or employee, but simply describes something lacking any activity

explanation.surface: Someone retired from service, such as an officer on the reserve list.
explanation.definitionFit: Something motionless and unreactive cannot be counted among the active.

parts.note: a happy beggar would wear happy tatters; the phrase for one's best clothes splits into a word for cheerful and a word for a beggar's clothing

explanation.surface: A question about what a happy vagrant might pretend or take on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assumed' means put on, as clothes are; a beggar wears rags, and a cheerful one wears glad ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for one's finest clothes, the outfit put on for a special occasion.

clue.text: They show what to expect at any stage

definitions.text: They show what to expect at any stage

parts.words: They show what to expect at any stage
parts.note: 'at any stage' sounds like 'at any point in time' but means on any theatre stage

explanation.surface: Something like a timetable or forecast covering every step of a process.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre posters and programmes announce the performance and cast coming to the boards.

parts.note: the name of a cue game played on a table sounds as if it ought to take place in water

explanation.surface: A plain statement that some sport is played on dry land.
explanation.definitionFit: The table game played with cues and pockets shares its name with a body of water, yet involves none.

parts.note: 'firm' looks like a company issuing statements about its policies, but here it means confident promises, and the same word names life insurance policies

explanation.surface: A company publishing official statements about its insurance products.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm pledges are promises given confidently, and the same plural word covers life-cover policies in British usage.

parts.note: to proscribe something is to ban it
an is the indefinite article
a is the other form of the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Outlawing certain items, which turns out productively.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'articles', supplies two pieces: AN and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellow tropical fruit is a literally fruity outcome of the construction.

clue.text: Oxford has more degrees in this than Cambridge

definitions.text: Oxford has more degrees in this than Cambridge

parts.words: Oxford has more degrees in this than Cambridge
parts.note: sounds like a boast about university qualifications, but the degrees are those measured east or west of Greenwich, and Oxford lies further west

explanation.surface: A rivalry claim that one ancient university awards more qualifications in some subject.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford is about 1.3 degrees west of Greenwich; Cambridge is almost on the meridian.
explanation.definitionFit: Angular distance east or west of the prime meridian is counted in degrees.

clue.text: Shake this weapon, Ian, like music, Will

definitions.text: Shake this weapon, Ian, like music, Will

parts.words: Shake this weapon, Ian, like music, Will
parts.note: putting 'Shake' before the weapon gives the playwright Will's surname, and adding 'Ian' gives the adjective used for music set to his plays

explanation.surface: Someone urging a person named Ian to brandish a weapon musically, like Will.
explanation.walkthrough: Shake + weapon is the Bard's name; add -IAN for the adjective; Will is William, his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A long pointed throwing or thrusting weapon is the thing one could shake.

clue.text: Teardrops from them? From their victims, more likely

definitions.text: Teardrops from them? From their victims, more likely

parts.words: Teardrops from them? From their victims, more likely
parts.note: the letters of 'teardrops' rearrange into the answer, yet it is the prey of these hunters, not the hunters, who would shed tears

explanation.surface: A wry correction: the tears come not from the attackers but from those they attack.
explanation.walkthrough: TEARDROPS is an exact anagram of the answer, so the tears come 'from them' in letters; in life they come from their prey.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that hunt and kill others are the ones whose prey might weep.

clue.text: Such a word is coined occasionally

definitions.text: Such a word is coined occasionally

parts.words: Such a word is coined occasionally
parts.note: 'occasionally' sounds like 'now and then' but means for one particular occasion only

explanation.surface: A remark that new words get invented from time to time.
explanation.definitionFit: A word made up for a single occasion is known by this term.

clue.text: This club is not for revolutionaries

definitions.text: This club is not for revolutionaries

parts.words: This club is not for revolutionaries
parts.note: a respectable service club for businesspeople, whose name nonetheless means revolving

explanation.surface: A society that bars radicals from membership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionaries' suggests rebels; the club's name means turning round and round.
explanation.definitionFit: The international service club for business leaders is named for rotating meetings between members' offices.

clue.text: Border the scene of fighting? That's right

definitions.text: Border the scene of fighting? That's right

parts.words: Border the scene of fighting? That's right
parts.note: a boundary between countries, often where battles happen; 'front' for a battle zone sits inside the word

explanation.surface: Someone confirming that a border region was where the war was fought.
explanation.walkthrough: The word begins with FRONT, the line where armies fight, and means a border.
explanation.definitionFit: A national boundary is the border line between two states.

clue.text: He admits that is his job

definitions.text: He admits that is his job

parts.words: He admits that is his job
parts.note: 'admits' sounds like confessing, but means letting people in through an entrance

explanation.surface: A man confessing what his work is.
explanation.definitionFit: A porter at an entrance lets visitors in as his duty.

parts.note: swing suggests a jazz style, but here it is a ride, and the music is the organ of a travelling funfair

explanation.surface: A question about a venue for jazz of the big band era.
explanation.definitionFit: A funfair site has swings and rides accompanied by loud music.

definitions.meaning: integrity read as wholeness: someone not whole is only in part, so the phrase becomes 'I am partial'

explanation.surface: A confession of dishonesty that ends with a claim of fairness.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as I'M PARTIAL: 'I lack integrity' means I am not whole, but in parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair judge treats both sides equally, showing no favour.

parts.note: a slang word for clothes also means failures that do not work, as with shells that fail to explode

explanation.surface: Garments obviously meant for leisure rather than labour.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal term for clothes is also slang for things that are useless or fail to function.

clue.text: Ships RN chooses to be reviewed …

indicators.note: to be reviewed means looked over again, so these letters are reorganised

explanation.surface: The Royal Navy selects which vessels will parade at a fleet inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be reviewed' rearranges RN CHOOSES; the surface plays on a naval fleet review.
explanation.definitionFit: Fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessels with two or more masts are a type of ship.

clue.text: … here? Point to top of mine

parts.note: S is the compass point south
the pithead is the top of a mine shaft

explanation.surface: Continuing the naval scene: pointing someone to the head of a coal mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here?' carries on from the clue above: the anchorage off Portsmouth where Royal Navy fleet reviews are held.
explanation.definitionFit: This stretch of the Solent off Portsmouth is the traditional place where the Royal Navy holds fleet reviews.

parts.note: putting the word before 'cat' gives the term for an imitator, and to ape is to imitate

explanation.surface: An odd claim that some feline looks like a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ape' is a verb here, to mimic, not an animal; a copycat imitates.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to imitate or reproduce what they do.

clue.text: Contradiction of idea that money talks? Right

definitions.text: Contradiction of idea that money talks?
definitions.meaning: if money talks, speaking costs money; the opposite is talking at no cost
a civil liberty guaranteed to citizens

explanation.surface: A rebuttal of the cynical saying that wealth buys influence, briefly affirmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberty of expression is a civil right, and also the no-cost talk that would refute the saying.

parts.note: sounds like a pension or annuity, but is the money demanded to spare a kidnap victim

explanation.surface: Something like a lifelong pension or annuity.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidnappers demand this sum to release, and so spare, their captive.

clue.text: Menace low card, mainly with a higher one

indicators.note: mainly means most of the word is kept, here losing its last letter

parts.note: a three is a low playing card
a ten is a higher playing card

explanation.surface: A card player intimidating opponents with a weak card backed by a stronger one.
explanation.definitionFit: To menace someone is to intimidate them with harm.

parts.note: Iago in Othello says 'Who steals my purse steals' worthless rubbish

explanation.surface: A question about the wallet of Shakespeare's villain.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago's line is 'Who steals my purse steals trash'.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago dismisses his purse as worthless rubbish, the very word he uses.

clue.text: Way you see sound firm which goes to the wall

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: sound means the words 'you see' are spoken, giving two letters that say them

parts.note: U and C are the letters that say these two words
Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A firm, apparently explained in speech, that goes bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' turns 'you see' into the letters U C; 'goes to the wall' suggests going bust but means plaster applied to walls.
explanation.definitionFit: This plaster is applied as a coating to exterior walls.

parts.note: an Albert is a heavy fob linking a pocket watch to a waistcoat, named after Prince Albert; it sounds like a man named Albert keeping guard

explanation.surface: A man called Albert standing sentry.
explanation.definitionFit: An Albert is a type of linked metal strap for a pocket watch.

parts.note: a woman's name that is also the coloured ring of the eye, broken in the middle by the black opening at its centre

explanation.surface: A teacher being interrupted by a student in class.
explanation.definitionFit: The coloured part of the eye surrounds, and is broken by, the pupil.

clue.text: Shaw for example (as assumed by Lawrence)

definitions.text: Shaw for example (as assumed by Lawrence)

parts.words: Shaw for example (as assumed by Lawrence)
parts.note: T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the false name Shaw

explanation.surface: A remark about a writer named Shaw and another named Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw suggests George Bernard Shaw, but it is the name T. E. Lawrence (of Arabia) took on.
explanation.definitionFit: A false name adopted to hide identity, as Lawrence did.

parts.note: the word starts with porter, a dark beer, but means the fee a carrier charges

explanation.surface: A bill for transport that excludes the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Porter is a dark beer; the word's -AGE ending makes a fee for portering, nothing to do with drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A fee paid for having goods carried by a bearer.

parts.note: sterling suggests fine character, but here it means the silver standard that official stamps certify

explanation.surface: A tribute to people of excellent character.
explanation.definitionFit: Assay office stamps certify the purity of precious metal, and figuratively mark distinctive qualities.

parts.note: de is French for of

indicators.note: repelling means pushing back, so the word for evil is turned round

parts.note: sin is evil

explanation.surface: A missionary who converted the French by driving out wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repelling' signals the reversal. St Denis, patron saint of France and first bishop of Paris, is credited with converting the Gauls.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Denis was the missionary bishop who brought Christianity to Paris, a converter of souls.
